definition: A subfield of interpretability that seeks to reverse-engineer the specific computations and algorithms implemented by a neural network's internal components (neurons, circuits, attention heads).
details: Mechanistic interpretability treats a trained model somewhat like a compiled program to be reverse-engineered, aiming to identify human-understandable 'circuits' that implement specific capabilities or behaviors.

explainer.lead: Mechanistic interpretability reverse-engineers the specific computations that a neural network's neurons, circuits and attention heads implement. It matters because it aims to explain behaviour in terms of human-understandable mechanisms rather than correlations.

tiers.eli5: It is like taking apart a compiled program to see which little parts do which job, so you can explain why the whole thing behaves as it does.
tiers.practitioner: Researchers identify circuits and components tied to particular capabilities, treating the trained model like compiled code to be unpacked. A pitfall is that circuits found in one model or setting may not generalise to others.
tiers.paperLevel: The field seeks to identify human-understandable circuits implementing specific capabilities or behaviours within internal components. Definitions are qualitative; there is no single formal metric.

explainer.example: Analysts isolate a set of attention heads that together perform a specific task, such as copying a token from earlier in the sequence.
